case_study_insert.main_stem: Velvet Finch (VF) is a private limited company in the independent fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 28. Founded in 2013 by Isla Marchetti, the business runs a single boutique in the market town of Wexley and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. VF plans to invest $780,000 in a second boutique and a new e-commerce channel, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $330,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $24 a unit and a selling price of $42, and currently produces 19,000 units a year. VF faces a serious operational problem: inventory shrinkage has reached 4.6% of stock purchases through shoplifting and till errors.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 420 Wexley shoppers found that 58% would buy VF clothing online if next-day delivery were offered, and 47% had visited a rival boutique in the last year. Average transaction value is $74, with dresses priced $58-$95 the top-selling category at 9,200 units last year. The returns rate stands at 9% of units sold, and 34% of respondents said sustainable fabrics would make them choose VF over competitors. Weekly footfall is 1,850 customers, and the proposed second store location scored 7.6 out of 10 for visibility and access.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Velvet Finch as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, the fourth rise this year, increasing repayments on variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.10 to $12.81 per hour from April 2026, lifting retailers' wage bills. (3) Cotton and linen input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year and fashion-price inflation is 6.2%, while consumer spending on clothing grew 2.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: VF intends to fund part of the second boutique and e-commerce launch from retained profit. Explain two advantages for VF of using retained profit rather than the $450,000 ten-year bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs VF nothing in interest or repayments, which protects cash flow and the $42 selling price at a time when fixed costs are $216,000 a year. Every dollar of profit not paid as loan interest can absorb the 9.8% rise in cotton and linen input costs, so VF can hold its $58-$95 dress price points and defend the $74 average transaction value without a bank dictating repayment dates or lender conditions on the new store fit-out.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and recovery risk attached to the $450,000 bank loan, so the second boutique and e-commerce channel are not at risk of repossession if footfall disappoints or the 9% returns rate drags on margins. It also preserves full ownership and the freedom of laissez-faire leadership, letting Isla Marchetti deploy the $330,000 immediately, without bank consent for hiring the 28-person team or for later expansion decisions — important when the boutique trades on personal service and the second store must feel like the original, not a replica. VF can also time the retained-profit drawdown around seasonal peaks rather than serving a rigid monthly repayment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Velvet Finch, its expansion decision and its costs.

questions.question_text: VF is launching its second boutique and online store. Consider a social media influencer campaign, a local radio sponsorship, or print advertising in a regional fashion magazine. Which should VF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Social media influencer campaign: Fashion and lifestyle influencers with strong regional reach would put VF's dresses directly in front of the 47% of Wexley shoppers who already use rival boutiques and the 58% who said they would buy VF clothing online. Costs are modest, results are measurable in clicks and promo-code redemptions, and sustainable-fabric messaging can be woven into content for the 34% of respondents who prefer responsible sourcing. The risk is that influencer credibility varies and results compound over weeks rather than instantly.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio reaches a broad local audience during commuting hours and suits time-limited launch messages for the Wexley catchment. However, it is one-way communication with no visual merchandising of the dresses, wastes spend on listeners outside the trading area, and offers no click-through to the online store, limiting its power to drive both boutique footfall and e-commerce orders.

Print advertising in a regional fashion magazine: Print offers prestige and full-page visuals of the new range, but circulation is declining, readership cannot be matched to the shopper segments VF's own research identifies, and there is no measurable click-through, making it hard to attribute the $74 basket uplift to the spend. Cost per reached shopper is high for a 28-person business funding a $780,000 expansion.

Recommendation: VF should choose a social media influencer campaign. It targets the exact shopper segments identified in its research, costs a fraction of print or radio, delivers measurable online and boutique conversion, and reinforces the sustainability story valued by 34% of respondents. Radio is rejected as one-way and untargeted for fashion visuals, and print is rejected for declining, unmeasurable reach; VF can add posters in its existing storefront to support opening weekend.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to VF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of VF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and print advertising are rejected.

questions.question_text: VF operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. Explain two benefits for VF of laissez-faire leadership in motivating its boutique and e-commerce team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives VF's experienced stylists and online merchandisers genuine freedom to curate collections, set window displays and reply to customer queries in their own voice. This satisfies esteem and self-actualisation needs (Maslow), raising job satisfaction and loyalty so the 28-person team stays rather than costing VF recruitment fees and lost local knowledge, and it empowers staff to create the in-store theatre that draws the 1,850 weekly visitors past the till.

Point 2: A flat structure means staff communicate directly with Isla Marchetti without intermediaries, so styling ideas, complaints about the 9% returns rate and suggestions for reducing the 4.6% inventory shrinkage reach the owner quickly. Creative staff who feel trusted take more ownership of stock and tills, flagging shoplifting patterns and till errors early, which directly attacks the 4.6% shrinkage problem more cheaply than extra surveillance hires. It also suits a 28-person team where everyone knows the regulars by sight: staff spot unfamiliar faces, repeat offenders and unusual refund requests instantly, and sharing sell-through knowledge — which $58-$95 dresses moved fastest this week — keeps reordering tight so the right sizes stay on the boutique floor.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VF's team, shrinkage, footfall and leadership style.

questions.question_text: VF wants to cut its 4.6% inventory shrinkage and lift staff effort. Consider introducing a commission on sales or a profit-sharing scheme. Which should VF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Commission on sales: A percentage of each sale would directly reward selling effort, raise average basket value above $74, and suit the boutique's competitive service culture. It is simple to calculate and visible to staff every week. However, commission rewards revenue rather than loss prevention: staff would have no incentive to confront shoplifters, audit stock or report till errors, so the 4.6% shrinkage could worsen even as sales rise. It could also encourage overselling at busy periods, pushing customers toward returns, which already run at 9% of units sold.

Profit-sharing scheme: Sharing a portion of annual profit, with the distribution linked partly to a stock-loss target, aligns every member of the 28-person team behind protecting inventory. Staff gain a direct financial reason to watch the shop floor, challenge suspicious behaviour and keep tills accurate, and it reinforces the trust laissez-faire leadership depends on. Drawbacks are that the reward arrives once a year, weakening its motivational pull for short-term effort, and that staff may see payouts as small or unequal if measured loosely; it also needs transparent profit reporting in a private limited company.

Decision: VF should choose a profit-sharing scheme with a shrinkage-reduction condition attached to the annual payment. It targets the real problem (4.6% of stock purchases lost), rewards collective vigilance rather than individual selling pressure, and costs only when profit is actually made, protecting cash during the $780,000 expansion. Commission is rejected because it incentivises sales volume while ignoring the loss problem, risks clashing with the low-pressure styling service VF prides itself on, and could inflate the 9% returns rate further; VF can review commission for top stylists next year if conversion rates lag.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivation methods with limited application to VF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of one or both schemes in the context of VF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both schemes in the context of VF with a well-justified decision explaining why a sales commission is rejected and profit-sharing with a loss condition is preferred.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $216,000 ÷ ($42 − $24) = $216,000 ÷ $18.00 = 12,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 12,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $42 − $24 = $18.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $18.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. VF's managers can compare the 12,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 19,000 units, confirming a margin of safety of 7,000 units, and test whether the second boutique needs a further uplift to justify the $780,000 expansion before committing.
2. The $18.00 contribution per unit lets managers model promotional pricing, for example a 10% boutique sale at $37.80 would cut contribution to $13.80, showing exactly how many extra units must be sold to still cover the $216,000 fixed costs during the launch month.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $216,000 and contribution per unit, managers can check the $450,000 bank loan repayments are serviceable from store surplus and set profit targets for the new store manager, protecting cash while the e-commerce channel ramps up.
4. Managers can compute the unit cost ($216,000 ÷ 19,000 units = $11.37, plus $24 = $35.37 a unit) and track it quarterly alongside the 4.6% shrinkage rate to spot whether losses are eroding margins, and to press suppliers over the 9.8% cotton and linen inflation hitting the $24 variable cost.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 12,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $18.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 7,000 units vs 19,000-unit output; sale-price modelling vs $216,000 fixed costs; loan-service feasibility for the $450,000 bank loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $35.37 to track the 4.6% shrinkage.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has VF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.91 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.17 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.81 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.04 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $260,000 inventories + $90,000 trade receivables + $100,000 cash = $450,000; 2025 current assets = $295,000 + $120,000 + $150,000 = $565,000. 2024 cover = $450,000 ÷ $235,000 current liabilities = 1.91; 2025 cover = $565,000 ÷ $260,000 = 2.17. 2024 liquid cover = ($450,000 − $260,000) ÷ $235,000 = $190,000 ÷ $235,000 = 0.81; 2025 liquid cover = ($565,000 − $295,000) ÷ $260,000 = $270,000 ÷ $260,000 = 1.04.

Evaluation: VF's liquidity has clearly improved. The headline cover strengthened from 1.91 to 2.17 because cash ($100,000 to $150,000, +50.0%) grew faster than trade receivables ($90,000 to $120,000, +33.3%) while inventories rose only modestly from $260,000 to $295,000 ahead of the new store opening. Crucially, the measure excluding inventories moved from 0.81 to 1.04, so VF can now meet short-term debts without forced stock sales — essential while it services a $450,000 bank loan and funds a $780,000 expansion with non-current assets up from $1,480,000 to $1,960,000. However, inventories still absorbed $295,000, and receivables rose by a third to $120,000, so VF should monitor the drivers of the extra $30,000 of receivables and avoid over-stocking launch ranges for the second boutique.

Conclusion: VF's financial position has improved. Both cover measures rose, and the liquid measure crossed 1.00 in 2025, removing reliance on inventory sales to settle suppliers. The improvement is genuine, not cosmetic; VF should scrutinise whatever is driving the extra $30,000 of trade receivables and keep shrinkage at 4.6% or below so the stronger liquidity converts into sustainable profit for the second boutique.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liability movements and a justified conclusion on whether VF's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VF of launching the e-commerce channel alongside the second boutique.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The e-commerce channel lets VF sell beyond the Wexley catchment to the 58% of surveyed shoppers who said they would buy online with next-day delivery, and to younger buyers drawn by sustainable-fabric messaging that 34% of respondents value. It spreads fixed costs of $216,000 across more units sold, lifts the $74 average basket value through online exclusives, and generates direct customer data for promotions without paying for further leases.

Disadvantage: Online fulfilment adds picking, packing, courier and returns costs, and VF's 9% returns rate could prove even higher online where fit and fabric cannot be checked, eroding the $18.00 contribution per unit. It also needs website build, photography and stock integration within the $330,000 retained profit earmarked for the launch, and may cannibalise core boutique sales if the two channels are not priced and promoted coherently under VF's laissez-faire structure.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VF's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in input costs will affect VF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (from 4.25% to 5.0%): VF's $450,000 ten-year bank loan, if variable-rate, costs roughly 0.75% more a year, about $3,375 extra annual interest, marginally lifting the $216,000 fixed-cost burden. Higher rates also make consumers more cautious with discretionary clothing spending, though clothing spending still grew 2.8%, and raise the cost of any top-up borrowing for the second boutique fit-out. The direct cash impact is real but small, and VF can reduce it by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.9% rise to $12.81 per hour from April 2026): Every hourly-paid staff member at VF moves from $12.10 to $12.81 — shown arithmetic, $0.71 more per hour, a 5.9% rise recurring on every shift of all 28 staff across the boutique floor, e-commerce fulfilment and tills. The insert gives no payroll-hours figure, so the exact annual cash cost cannot be computed, but this rise recurs every hour VF trades and cannot be removed by one refinancing or one supplier negotiation. Because laissez-faire leadership keeps staffing flexible rather than automated, offsets must come from productivity gains, cross-training and modest price adjustments on $58-$95 dresses.

Input-cost inflation (9.8% rise in cotton and linen): Wholesale garment costs feed directly into VF's $24 variable cost per unit. The insert does not split the $24 between materials and labour, so the exact cash impact cannot be computed; even so, a full 9.8% on the entire variable cost is a shown-arithmetic upper bound of $2.35 a unit (9.8% × $24 = $2.352), about $44,688 a year on 19,000 units ($2.352 × 19,000), squeezing the $18.00 contribution per unit well below budget. In reality only the cotton-and-linen component is exposed, so the true impact sits below that bound — but it is still recurring and unavoidable without renegotiation or selective price rises.

Conclusion: The 5.9% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact on VF. It recurs permanently on every hour worked by all 28 staff, cannot be fixed, renegotiated away or hedged, and lands on the shop floor that drives the $74 average basket value — whereas the interest-rate rise costs only $3,375 a year (0.75% × $450,000, computed) and the input-cost rise, though up to an upper bound of about $44,688 a year on the whole $24 variable cost, in practice applies only to the exposed cotton-and-linen component and can partly be recovered in price. VF should respond with flexible rostering, multiskilling and a small, targeted price rise on best-selling dresses, while fixing its loan rate and pressing suppliers to blunt the next-biggest threat.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VF with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
